summary: Registers a Telephone Number Mapping (ENUM) service for presence, focusing on provisioning pres URIs in ENUM. This lets a phone number be mapped to a presence address.

plainLanguage.summary: You type a phone number into a special directory and it points you to the place online where you can see if that person is available.

questions: how does enum find presence information
subtitle: How a phone number in DNS can point to the address where that person's presence can be checked.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps telephone numbers to URIs, but there was no registered ENUM service for finding the presence information (online, busy, away) tied to a phone number.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the 'E2U+pres' enumservice. An ENUM record with this service holds a 'pres' URI, which is a generic pointer to a presence service.
tldr.outcome: A phone with an address book can look up a number, find the pres URI and then ask for the person's availability. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 3953 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: ENUM and Presence
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping, RFC 3761) uses DNS to translate a telephone number such as +12025332600 into a URI such as pres:user@host.com. It exists mainly to connect systems that rely on telephone numbers with systems that identify things by URI.

Presence, as defined in RFC 2778, lets users of a communications service watch one another's availability: online or offline, busy or idle, away from devices or nearby. The IETF defined the pres URI scheme (in the Common Profile for Presence, RFC 3859) to identify a presence service for a resource. This RFC describes an enumservice for advertising presence information tied to an E.164 number.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM is a phone book that gives you internet addresses instead of phone numbers. This RFC adds a new kind of entry: where to find out if the person is around.

sections.title: Watchers, Presentities and Presence States
sections.content:
Following the framework of RFC 2778, endpoints in a presence system are watchers and presentities. Watchers subscribe to the presence of presentities and are told when it changes. Watchers usually follow a group of presentities they have an ongoing relationship with.

The RFC gives a telephony example: a cellular phone has an address book of names and numbers, and could act as a watcher for some or all of those numbers. Selecting a presence-enabled number would show how available the destination is, so the user could adjust their calling habits.

The shared presence information depends on the service. The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF, RFC 3863) baseline declares only two states, OPEN and CLOSED: the first suggests the destination can accept communication requests, the second that it cannot. PIDF is extensible, so a telephony service could define a 'busy' status, but extending PIDF for telephony is outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A watcher is like a kid checking whether a friend's porch light is on. The light only says on or off, but other signs could be invented, like 'busy'.

sections.title: The E2U+pres Enumservice
sections.content:
Normally the services field of a NAPTR record (RFC 3403) has two subfields: a protocol and a resolution service. ENUM defines an E2U (E.164 to URI) resolution service. This RFC defines the E2U+pres enumservice for presence.

The URI in the regexp field of such a record SHOULD use the pres scheme. Other URI schemes appropriate to presence MAY be used, but pres gives greater compatibility than a URI tied to one particular presence protocol.

A pres URI does not name the protocol used for subscriptions and notifications. Instead, the mechanism in RFC 3861 discovers whether the presence protocols the watcher supports are also supported by the presentity. SIP (RFC 3261) is one protocol that can carry presence information and manage subscriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory entry holds a general-purpose address. Later, the two sides figure out which language they both speak, like picking a common language before chatting.

sections.title: Example Record
sections.content:
The RFC shows one NAPTR record using the new enumservice. It sits under the domain derived from the telephone number and holds a regular expression that rewrites any input to a fixed pres URI.

Looking up the number in DNS returns this record. The watcher then reads the pres URI from it and uses the resolution techniques of RFC 3861 to reach a presence service.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one phone-book line that says: for this number, the presence address is this name at this website.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
DNS makes no policy decisions about who may see a record, so all records must be assumed available to everyone, all the time. An ENUM record set is therefore public, which raises some privacy concerns.

Revealing a pres URI is unlikely to cause many problems, though depending on its structure it might reveal the target's full name or employer. Anonymous URIs reduce this risk. The more serious concern is unauthorized distribution of presence information itself. Presence protocols have security requirements (RFC 2779) calling for authentication of watchers, integrity and confidentiality, and any presence protocol used with the pres scheme is required to meet them.

Unlike a plain telephone number, a pres URI target may demand cryptographic credentials before it returns presence data. The RFC says that, together with presence protocols, ENUM can give far greater protection from unwanted callers than the existing PSTN, even though ENUM records are public.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read the phone book, so the book only says where to ask. The place it points to can still ask who you are before it answers.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
The registration is made in the enumservice registry described in RFC 3761. Its template fields are:

  • Service name: E2U+pres
  • URI scheme: pres:
  • Intended usage: COMMON
  • Functional specification: section 4; security considerations: section 6

The author listed is Jon Peterson.
